lead: Signal conditioning turns a weak, noisy, non-linear sensor output into a clean standard voltage or current that the next stage can digitise safely. A strain gauge may give only 2 mV at full load; an ADC needs volts. Conditioning amplifies, filters, linearises and isolates. It also attenuates large signals and matches impedance so a high-resistance sensor is not loaded. You meet it in PLC input cards, data loggers, medical front ends and every industrial transmitter that sends 4-20 mA to a control room.
prereq: You need: sensitivity, linearity and accuracy from Unit 1, and the strain-gauge bridge output from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A sensor output is small and often sits on a larger offset. An amplifier multiplies the difference by a fixed gain. For the difference amplifier in the worked example, gain is set by two resistors: G = R<sub>f</sub> / R<sub>in</sub>. Here R<sub>f</sub> is feedback resistance in ohms and R<sub>in</sub> is input resistance in ohms. With R<sub>f</sub> = 100 kΩ and R<sub>in</sub> = 200 Ω, G = 500. The same gain in decibels is G<sub>dB</sub> = 20 log₁₀(G) = 20 log₁₀(500) = 54.0 dB. dB is a ratio, not a voltage.
G = R<sub>f</sub> / R<sub>in</sub>,   G<sub>dB</sub> = 20 log₁₀(G),   V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> × R₂/(R₁+R₂)
blocks.where: G is voltage gain, no unit; R<sub>f</sub> is feedback resistance in Ω; R<sub>in</sub> is input resistance in Ω; G<sub>dB</sub> is gain in decibels; V<sub>out</sub> and V<sub>in</sub> are voltages in V; R₁ and R₂ are divider resistors in Ω.

blocks.text: An instrumentation amplifier is three op-amps in one package. It has high input impedance, so it does not load a bridge, and it rejects the voltage common to both inputs. That common voltage may be 2.5 V of offset while the signal is 2 mV. A plain op-amp difference circuit with low input resistance would draw current from the bridge and reduce the signal. Some syllabi call the whole chain signal conditioning and processing.

Large signals need attenuation, not gain. A resistive divider gives V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> × R₂/(R₁+R₂). Impedance matching means the next stage input resistance is much larger than the source resistance, often at least 10 times. A pH electrode may have 100 MΩ source resistance, so a 1 MΩ ADC input would load it badly.

Mains hum at 50 Hz, switching supplies at 20 kHz and radio pickup add to the signal. A first-order RC low-pass filter passes low frequencies and attenuates high ones. It uses a resistor R in ohms and capacitor C in farads. The cutoff frequency is f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πRC). At f<sub>c</sub> the output falls to 1/√2 = 0.707 of the input, a drop of 3 dB. Above f<sub>c</sub> the gain falls by about 20 dB per decade.

Magnitude: |V<sub>out</sub>/V<sub>in</sub>| = 1/√(1+(f/f<sub>c</sub>)²). Here f is the signal frequency in hertz. With R = 10 kΩ and C = 1 µF, RC = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁶ = 0.01 s, so f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2π × 0.01) = 15.9 Hz. That removes 50 Hz hum but also cuts a fast strain pulse. Pick f<sub>c</sub> above the highest real signal frequency and below the noise.

A filter is not a magic cleaner. It adds delay and phase shift. For a step input it gives a slow exponential rise with time constant τ = RC = 0.01 s. For 50 Hz hum at a 15.9 Hz cutoff, the attenuation is 1/√(1+(50/15.9)²) = 0.303, about -10.4 dB, so a 1 V hum becomes 0.303 V. Filters with sharper cutoffs are in 6.9.

Many sensors are not straight lines. A thermocouple output is a small polynomial in temperature; a thermistor resistance falls exponentially. Linearisation makes the conditioned output proportional to the measured quantity. A breakpoint circuit compares the input with several reference voltages. Between two breakpoints it adds a slope correction. The straight line between points (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is y = y₁ + (y₂-y₁)(x-x₁)/(x₂-x₁). Here x is the raw sensor signal and y is the corrected output.

Software linearisation stores a lookup table of raw ADC counts against known temperatures. Between table entries it interpolates with the same formula. It is cheap and accurate if the table is calibrated. A thermistor is often linearised with one fixed parallel resistor over a narrow range, or with a table over a wide range. A thermocouple needs cold-junction compensation first; that is in Unit 2.

Electrical isolation breaks the direct current path between the sensor side and the computer side. A transformer isolates AC signals; an opto-coupler uses an LED and phototransistor for digital or slow analogue signals. Isolation stops ground loops, where two earth points at slightly different voltages drive a current through the signal cable. It also protects the ADC from surges on a long cable. An isolation amplifier has a rating, say 2.5 kV, meaning the safe voltage between its two sides.

Attenuation and impedance matching also belong here. A 0-10 V transmitter feeding a 3.3 V ADC needs a divider. A 4-20 mA current loop uses a 250 Ω resistor to make 1-5 V; the current is the same along the loop, so cable resistance does not spoil it. Transmission is covered in 6.3.

figure.caption: A 2 mV sensor signal gets gain 500 and an about 16 Hz low-pass filter, then linearisation and isolation, before a standard 0-5 V output. Notice how each block repairs one defect of the raw signal.

spec.title: Signal conditioning chain
spec.aria: A left-to-right chain from a 2 mV sensor through a gain-500 amplifier, a 16 Hz low-pass filter, a lineariser and an isolator to a 0-5 V output.

examples.question: A strain-gauge bridge gives 2 mV at full load. A difference amplifier uses R<sub>f</sub> = 100 kΩ and R<sub>in</sub> = 200 Ω. Find the voltage gain, the amplifier output, and the cutoff frequency of a first-order RC low-pass filter with R = 10 kΩ and C = 1 µF that follows it. Also give the gain in dB.
steps: Voltage gain: G = R<sub>f</sub>/R<sub>in</sub> = 100 kΩ / 200 Ω = 100000/200 = 500.
Amplifier output: V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> × G = 2 mV × 500 = 1000 mV = 1.0 V.
Gain in dB: G<sub>dB</sub> = 20 log₁₀(500) = 20 × 2.699 = 53.98 dB ≈ 54.0 dB.
Filter time constant: τ = RC = 10 kΩ × 1 µF = 10⁴ Ω × 10⁻⁶ F = 0.01 s.
examples.answer: The gain is 500 (54.0 dB), the amplifier output is 1.0 V, and the filter cutoff is 15.9 Hz.
examples.check:
import math
vin_mV = 2.0
Rf = 100e3
Rin = 200.0
R = 10e3
C = 1e-6
gain = Rf / Rin
vout = vin_mV * 1e-3 * gain
gain_db = 20 * math.log10(gain)
fc = 1 / (2 * math.pi * R * C)
print(round(gain, 1))
print(round(vout, 1))
print(round(gain_db, 1))
print(round(fc, 1))

traps: Gain multiplies offset drift and noise with the signal. A gain of 500 on 2 mV also makes 0.1 mV of input offset into 50 mV at the output; accuracy does not improve by gain alone.
dB is a ratio: 20 log₁₀(Vout/Vin). Do not write 500 dB for a voltage ratio of 500; it is about 54 dB.
In f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πRC), R must be in ohms and C in farads. Using 10 kΩ as 10 and 1 µF as 1 gives a wrong 0.0159 Hz.
Isolation stops ground loops and protects against surges; it does not fix a non-linear sensor or remove all noise. A dirty signal is still dirty after the isolator.
A low-pass filter cuts real fast changes as well as noise. Set f<sub>c</sub> above the signal bandwidth, or a step will be slowed with τ = RC.

quiz.q: State the four main jobs of signal conditioning.
quiz.a: Amplification (or attenuation), filtering, linearisation and electrical isolation.

quiz.q: Why is an instrumentation amplifier preferred to a simple op-amp difference amplifier for a strain-gauge bridge?
quiz.a: It has very high input impedance, so it does not load the bridge, and it has good common-mode rejection, so it removes the large offset shared by both bridge outputs while amplifying the small difference.

quiz.q: A sensor gives 5 mV. An amplifier has R<sub>f</sub> = 220 kΩ and R<sub>in</sub> = 1 kΩ. Find the gain, the output voltage and the gain in dB.
An RC low-pass filter has R = 4.7 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF. Find f<sub>c</sub> and the attenuation at 50 Hz.
A thermistor output is very non-linear. Compare a breakpoint circuit and a software lookup table for linearisation.
quiz.a: A breakpoint circuit uses hardware comparators and adds slope corrections; it is fast but limited to a few fixed segments. A lookup table is flexible and can hold many calibrated points, but needs memory, calibration data and interpolation code.

quiz.q: What is a ground loop and how does isolation break it?
quiz.a: A ground loop is a current path formed when two earth points are at slightly different voltages. Isolation breaks the direct current path with a transformer or opto-coupler, so no loop current can flow through the signal cable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern signal conditioning often sits in one chip: a programmable-gain amplifier, a sigma-delta ADC and a digital filter in the same package. Isolated amplifiers and opto-couplers are common in motor drives and medical devices for safety. Digital linearisation with calibration tables is standard in smart sensors. Search for programmable gain instrumentation amplifier, isolated amplifier, RTD linearisation and 4-20 mA transmitter.
